newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank revenues from derivatives rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank revenues from derivatives rise.

text.p: U.S. banks gained $7.5 billion in revenue from derivatives trading in 1996, up from $6.14 billion in all of 1995, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) said Thursday.
Fourth quarter revenues were $1.9 billion, up from $1.6 billion recorded in the fourth quarter of 1995, the banking regulator said.

The 1996 fourth quarter revenues comprised $990 million from interest rate positions ($879 million a year ago), $767 million from foreign exchange positions ($592 million), $109 million from equity, commodity and other positions ($95 million).
Notional volume of derivatives activity at commercial banks increased in the fourth quarter of 1996 to $20 trillion from $16.86 trillion in the same period a year earlier.
Notional amounts indicate the level of derivatives activity but do not necessarily reveal the amount banks have at risk, OCC said.

Banks notional value of interest rate contracts were $13.4 trillion in the fourth quarter ($11.1 trillion a year earlier), foreign exchange contracts notional value $6.24 trillion ($5.39 trillion), commodity and equity contracts $366 billion ($378 billion).

Off-balance sheet derivatives continued to be concentrated in the largest banks. Eight commercial banks account for 94 percent of the total notional amount with 98 percent accounted for by the top 25 banks.

Non-performing contracts remained at nominal levels in the fourth quarter. For all banks, the book value of contracts past due 30 days or more totaled only $3 million, or 0.001 percent of total credit exposure from derivatives contracts.

"These figures reflect both the current healthy economic environment and the relatively high credit quality of counterparties and end-users with whom banks presently engage in dervatives transactions, as well as the increased use of collateral," the OCC said.
